## Intent
Hypothesis: a Halide-scheduled branchless-blend integration loop can approach the streaming ceiling by keeping the death verdict in registers and avoiding intermediate storage.

## Layout & approach
The 68 B/particle AoS layout offers loop 1 a 47% hot fraction (32 of 68 B: age+pos+seed+vel) and loop 2 a 41% hot fraction (28 of 68 B: color+pos), meaning more than half of every cache line dragged through the filler is dead weight. With no intermediate storage, the death verdict stays in registers — no auxiliary array to stream. The expected advantage is a single fused pass with branchless blend keeping the pipeline steady; the expected cost is that the 53–59% dead bytes per line inflate the effective traffic and the scalar codegen (see below) cannot amortize them.

## Cache saturation
All measured points sit in L3-resident (N=10K–100K, working set 0.68–6.8 MB within the 16 MB L3) or DRAM (N=1M–10M, 68–680 MB). The ns/p curve is strikingly flat: 19.824 ns/p at N=10K L3 versus 20.562 ns/p at N=10M DRAM at q=0.01 — a mere 4% rise across the L3→DRAM transition. At q=0.5 the same flatness holds (24.98 → 26.126, ~5%). There is no cache-spill knee because the cost is not memory-latency-dominated; the 49–53% frontend stall swamps any DRAM penalty. The dense grid confirms: regime changes are invisible in ns/p.

## Bandwidth
The memory floor is 5.359 ns/p; actual ns/p ranges 19.824–26.546, or 3.7–5.0× the floor — only 20–27% of time is irreducible memory time. Achieved bandwidth peaks at 3.45 GB/s (q=0.01, N=100K) = 27% of the 12.69 GB/s ceiling, and bottoms at 2.56 GB/s (q=0.5, N=1M) = 20%. The algo is frontend/overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound. Against the naive scalar baseline it is slower everywhere: 0.78× at q=0.01 N=10K, degrading to 0.72× at q=0.5 N=10K. Against the winner (AF02.LP1-autovec.LP2-opt) it trails 2.572× at q=0.01 N=10K, narrowing to 1.384× at q=0.5 N=10M — the higher death rate erodes the winner's vectorization advantage but never closes the gap.

## Assembly
The histogram reports zero vector-suffixed instructions. The integration loop is entirely scalar: `vaddss`, `vmulss`, `vcvttss2si`, `vsubss` — one lane per op. A `call halide_b2` is preceded by a 1096-byte stack frame (`sub rsp,0x448`) and roughly 100 `mov QWORD PTR [rbp-…]` instructions marshaling arguments, which directly explains the 49–53% frontend stall. The death verdict itself is branchless (`setge`, `sets`, `setns`, `setle`, `or`, `and`, `test`), but respawn writeback is branchy (`jne`, `jbe`, `jae` per particle) and uses byte-granular scatter: `movzx` → `add` → `cmovb` → `mov BYTE PTR [r13+rdi*1+0x0]` repeated for each of three color channels. The `vpaddusb` and `vpextrb` instructions operate on packed bytes for color, not on particle vectors.

## Verdict
Refuted — 0.72–0.81× of the naive scalar baseline at every N×q point and 1.38–2.57× slower than the winner. The Halide schedule emitted scalar codegen (zero vector instructions) behind a 1096-byte stack-marshaling preamble that drives frontend stalls to 49–53%, while byte-granular color scatter and branchy respawn writeback prevent any streaming benefit. The branchless death verdict survived in registers as intended, but the surrounding codegen overhead makes the algo slower than hand-written scalar regardless of death rate.
